title: Mixing a rabbit feed ration at home
subtitle: Balancing hay, pellets, and fresh food for a working rabbit diet.
excerpt: Rabbits have a digestive system built around high-fibre, low-energy forage. A well-designed home ration keeps the hindgut microbiome healthy, prevents obesity, and reduces the risk of dental disease. Hay is always the bulk; pellets and fresh food are supplements, not the main meal.
sourceNotes: RSPCA, Diet of Rabbits (2023). Frances Harcourt-Brown, Textbook of Rabbit Medicine (2002), nutrition chapter. British Rabbit Council, Feeding and Nutrition (2022).

glossaryTerms.definition: The process by which rabbits re-ingest their soft caecal droppings (caecotropes), which are produced at night. These contain B vitamins and amino acids and are an essential part of the rabbit's nutrition.
Abnormal molar and incisor growth, very common in rabbits fed low-hay diets. The teeth grow continuously and require fibre wear to maintain correct alignment.

content.text: A well-fed rabbit spends most of the day eating hay. Unlimited meadow hay is not a luxury; it is the functional core of a rabbit's digestive health. A rabbit that eats less hay than it should, usually because it is filling up on pellets, is on a pathway toward gut stasis and
. Get the hay right before adjusting anything else.

Hay: unlimited, always available. Meadow hay or timothy hay is ideal. Legume hay (alfalfa, clover) is high in calcium and protein; suitable for young rabbits and pregnant does, not for adult maintenance.

Pellets: 1 tablespoon per kg of body weight per day for adults. A 2 kg adult rabbit gets 2 tablespoons. Use plain compressed pellets, not a muesli mix; rabbits pick out the sweet pieces from muesli and leave the fibre.

Fresh leafy greens: a large double handful per 2 kg bodyweight per day. Suitable varieties include dark-leafed lettuce, rocket, watercress, spinach, kale, and fresh herbs. Introduce any new green slowly to avoid digestive upset.
Kits from 3 weeks to 12 weeks: unlimited alfalfa hay and pellets. The rapid growth phase requires higher protein and calcium than adult maintenance.
Pregnant and nursing does: increase pellet ration by 50% and offer alfalfa hay alongside meadow hay. Nursing does have very high energy requirements.
Older rabbits (over 6 years): senior rabbits often lose weight and need pellet rations increased. Check bodyweight monthly.

, the re-ingestion of soft caecal droppings, happens at night when the rabbit is undisturbed. You rarely see it. What you may notice is a build-up of soft caecotropes stuck to the hindquarters: this usually means the rabbit is eating more pellets and greens than it needs, and the excess caecotropes go uneaten. Reduce pellet intake by 25% and see whether the problem resolves.
Iceberg lettuce: high water content and very low nutrition; causes loose droppings.
Dried fruit and sweet treats: high sugar disrupts hindgut flora.
Onion family (onion, leek, chives): toxic to rabbits.
Potato tops, rhubarb, and raw beans: all toxic.

attrs.cue: Rabbit is eating very little hay despite hay being always available
attrs.cause: Too full on pellets or greens, or dental discomfort making hay painful to chew
attrs.fix: Halve the pellet ration for 5 days and see if hay consumption rises. If it does not, have the rabbit's teeth checked by a vet experienced with rabbits.

attrs.cue: Soft caecotropes stuck to the rabbit's hindquarters
attrs.cause: Overfeeding pellets or greens; excess caecotropes produced but not consumed
attrs.fix: Reduce pellet intake by 25 to 30%. Check that the rabbit is not too obese to reach its hindquarters, which is a separate problem requiring weight reduction.
